764.title: Mindfulness of death
764.hook: the Buddha asks his monks how they recall death, and the answers shrink from a day to a single breath
764.howItsDone: Some Buddhists practice maranasati, mindfulness of death, as a regular recollection: some repeat a short reflection that life is uncertain and death is certain, others simply attend to each breath as if it were the one they can count on.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Montaigne hoped death would find him planting cabbages. Your line was learn to die. What ordinary thing did you do slowly? A new week, and Buddhist voices begin. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

A hall built of brick, and a group of monks seated in front of their teacher. The Buddha asks them a direct question: do you practice mindfulness of death? Yes, says one, and explains how. Yes, says another, and explains differently. And as they go around the room, something odd happens. The span of time each one names gets shorter and shorter, from a whole day, down to a meal, down to a mouthful, down to a single breath. The Buddha listens to all of them, and then tells them which ones have understood.
screen: `DO YOU RECALL DEATH?` → `EACH ANSWER GETS SHORTER.` → `DOWN TO ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Maranasati is Pali: marana, death, and sati, mindfulness. Mindfulness of death. In this discourse the Buddha says that when it is developed, it brings great fruit and leads toward the deathless. Second, the long spans. The first monk says he thinks: if only I might live one more day and night, I could attend to the teaching and do much. Another says the same about a single day. Another, as long as it takes to eat one meal. Another, while he chews and swallows a few mouthfuls of food. The Buddha's verdict on these is quiet but firm: they are living heedlessly. Their mindfulness of death is too slow. Third, the short spans. Then one monk says: just for the time it takes to chew and swallow one mouthful. And another: just for the time between breathing in and breathing out, or breathing out and breathing in. These two, the Buddha says, are heedful. They are developing mindfulness of death keenly. Fourth, why the breath. The point isn't fear. It's attention. A day feels long enough to put things off. A breath doesn't. If you only count on this breath, the next unkind word, the next put-off apology, the next thing you meant to notice, all of it is happening now or not at all. The Buddha ends by telling the monks to train this way: we will live heedfully. Some Buddhists today practice this recollection with a short phrase, some simply with the breath.
screen: `MARANA, DEATH; SATI, MINDFULNESS.` · `A DAY, A MEAL: TOO SLOW.` · `ONE MOUTHFUL, ONE BREATH.` · `NOT FEAR, ATTENTION.` · then, large: `THIS BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and breathe normally for a moment. Now take one breath as if it were the only one you could count on. Not dramatically. Just fully. Feel it come in, the cool at the nose, the rise of the chest. Feel it go out. That one breath, completely. Then the next breath, the same way. If the mind jumps ahead to later today, notice that it jumped, and come back to this breath. If the idea of a last breath feels heavy right now, drop it and simply attend to each breath as it comes. The bell holds the time.
Maranasati: Pali for mindfulness of death, practiced in the Buddha's teaching down to the span of a single breath. Today's word.
Your line: this breath. Today, when you catch yourself putting something kind off until later, take one full breath and do it now. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

what it means: recalling that only this breath is certain, so you live heedfully now.

765.title: The charnel ground
765.hook: monks once reflected on bodies left in the cemetery, and turned the reflection on themselves
765.howItsDone: In some Buddhist traditions, monastics and lay practitioners reflect on the body's impermanence using the charnel-ground contemplations, in words, images or cemetery visits, and teachers adapt or set them aside for people who are grieving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha's monks named shorter and shorter spans, down to one breath. Your line was this breath. Did you do one kind thing now instead of later? Today, a harder place to sit. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

Bones, bleached white, the color of shells. That's one of the images in an old Buddhist discourse on the foundations of mindfulness. It describes a charnel ground, an open field outside a town where bodies were left rather than buried. And it asks a monk to sit with what happens there, stage by stage, and then to turn and look at his own body. It is a hard text. Read slowly, it is also a strangely tender one, and it hands the monk one line to carry home.
screen: `BONES THE COLOR OF SHELLS.` → `A FIELD OUTSIDE THE TOWN.` → `THEN LOOK AT YOUR OWN BODY.`

segments.voice: First, the stages. In the Satipatthana discourse, the Buddha describes a monk who sees, or calls to mind, a body thrown aside in a charnel ground: one, two or three days dead, swollen, discolored. Then a body being eaten by crows and dogs and jackals. Then a skeleton, held together by sinews. Then bones scattered in every direction. Then bones white as shells, bones in a heap, bones crumbling to dust. The text doesn't hurry. It goes stage by stage. Second, the turn. After each picture comes the same move. The monk compares it with his own body, and reflects: this body too is of the same nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that. The point is not disgust at someone else. The point is to see his own body plainly, as one of all bodies. Third, why a body. In this discourse the reflection sits among other ways of attending to the body: the breath, and the postures of walking, standing, sitting and lying down. It's mindfulness, not morbidity. Seeing the body as it is, Buddhists say, loosens clinging to it, and to the fear that comes with that clinging. Fourth, taught gently. Some teachers today still offer the cemetery reflection, by a walk among graves, by images, or simply in words. Others set it aside for someone in fresh grief, or for someone with a hard history with their body. The text itself is strong medicine. Like any strong medicine, it's given with care, in a dose a person can take.
screen: `STAGE BY STAGE, TO DUST.` · `THIS BODY TOO IS OF THE SAME NATURE.` · `MINDFULNESS, NOT MORBIDITY.` · `STRONG MEDICINE, GIVEN WITH CARE.` · then, large: `ALL BODIES.`

segments.voice: This practice is a gentle version. Settle, and feel your body from the inside: the weight on the seat, the hands, the warmth of the chest, the breath moving. This body has carried you all your life. Now, quietly, add the discourse's line: this body too is of the same nature. Not as a threat. As a fact you share with everyone you love, everyone you pass on the street, all bodies. If that's too heavy today, simply feel the body breathing and leave the line aside. If you can, later this week, walk slowly through a cemetery. The bell holds the time.
Satipatthana, the Buddhist discourse on mindfulness that asks a monk to see his own body as one of all bodies. Today's word.
Your line: all bodies. Today, when you look at a stranger, remember once that their body and yours share the same nature, and let that soften how you meet them. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

766.title: Strive on
766.hook: the Buddha's last words: all component things decay; work on with diligence
766.carry: decay is inherent in all component things
766.howItsDone: Some Buddhists remember the Buddha's last words, recited in Pali, as a reminder of impermanence and a call to practice with heedfulness rather than delay.

segments.voice: Yesterday, satipatthana's charnel ground, and the line this body too is of the same nature. Your line was all bodies. Did a stranger look different for a moment? Today, the Buddha's own last night. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

Last words get repeated. People write them down, argue over them, carve them on stones. The long discourse on the Buddha's final days ends with his, spoken at night in a grove near a small town called Kusinara, lying between two sal trees, with his monks gathered close. They are not a blessing, not a promise, not a farewell. They are a short sentence of instruction, half fact and half job. Earlier, Ananda has gone aside to weep. The teacher is still teaching.
screen: `A GROVE AT NIGHT, TWO SAL TREES.` → `THE MONKS GATHERED CLOSE.` → `HE IS STILL TEACHING.`

segments.voice: First, no new teacher. Before the end, the Buddha tells Ananda that some may think: the word of the Master is over, we have no teacher anymore. Not so, he says. The teaching and the discipline he has given them will be their teacher after he is gone. Second, any doubts? He asks the monks whether any of them has a doubt or a question about the Buddha, the teaching, the path or the order. Ask now, he says, so you won't regret later that you didn't ask while the teacher was face to face with you. They are silent. He asks a second time, and a third. Silence. Third, the fact. Then come the last words. In T. W. Rhys Davids's old translation they read: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" The first half is the fact. Everything that is put together comes apart: bodies, plans, friendships, mountains, the teacher lying there in front of them. Nothing in the sentence softens that. Fourth, the job. The second half doesn't say: so despair. It says: so work. The Pali word Rhys Davids renders as diligence is appamada, the heedfulness the Buddha praised in the monks who recalled death with each breath. Other translators put the whole line more simply, as strive on, with heedfulness. Death is not the end of the sentence. Diligence is. The reason to remember that things fall apart, in this telling, is to use well the time they hold together.
screen: `THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.` · `ANY DOUBTS? ASKED THREE TIMES.` · `DECAY IS INHERENT IN ALL COMPONENT THINGS.` · `WORK OUT YOUR SALVATION WITH DILIGENCE.` · then, large: `STRIVE ON.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one small thing in your life that's half done. A message, a drawer, a form, a page, a repair. Something you could finish today. Picture it clearly, and notice why it's been waiting: tiredness, dread, distraction. Don't scold yourself. Just see it. Then hold the first half of the line, everything put together comes apart, and let it make the moment feel a little more precious than urgent. When the bell rings, get up and finish that one thing, with care, all the way. The bell holds the time.
Strive on: the Buddha's last instruction. All put-together things decay, so work on with diligence and heedfulness. Today's word.
Your line: decay is inherent in all component things. Today, finish one thing you've left half done, slowly and thoroughly, as if the time to do it well were a gift. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

767.title: No one to blame
767.hook: after his last meal, the Buddha tells Ananda no one should blame Cunda who cooked it
767.howItsDone: Buddhists remember Cunda's meal in retellings of the Buddha's last days, and the Buddha's message to him is read as a teaching on compassion and on not turning grief into blame.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha's last words: all conditioned things decay, so strive on. Your line was decay is inherent in all component things. Did you finish one thing? Today, a scene from a little earlier on that same last road. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.
screen: `DECAY IS INHERENT IN ALL COMPONENT THINGS.`

segments.voice: A meal goes wrong. In the long account of the Buddha's final journey, he stops at the mango grove of a smith named Cunda. Cunda cooks for him and his monks, glad to have them. After eating, the Buddha falls badly sick, with sharp pains, and still walks on toward the place where he will die. Somewhere behind him, a cook is about to hear that the last meal he served his teacher came just before the sickness. Today: what the Buddha does about the cook.
screen: `A SMITH NAMED CUNDA.` → `A MEAL, THEN SICKNESS.` → `WHAT ABOUT THE COOK?`

segments.voice: First, the dish. Before the meal, the text says, the Buddha asked Cunda to serve one particular dish only to him, and to bury whatever was left, because he saw no one else who could digest it. Readers still argue about what that dish was. Whatever it was, he kept the monks away from it. Second, the danger. Later, sick on the road, the Buddha tells Ananda, his attendant, that someone might stir up remorse in Cunda: telling him it was his loss, his fault, that the teacher died after eating his food. Third, the message. The Buddha asks Ananda to go to Cunda and say something else instead. Two offerings of food, he says, bear the same great fruit, above all others: the meal a Buddha eats before his awakening, and the meal he eats before his final passing. Cunda's meal isn't to be remembered as a mistake. It is named a gift. Fourth, what this does on an ordinary day. The sutta doesn't hide the order of events; the meal and the sickness sit side by side in the text. Buddhist teaching is full of causes. But here the Buddha won't let a cause become a culprit, and he spends some of his last strength on a cook's peace of mind. When someone dies, grief looks for a place to land: the doctor, the driver, the sister who didn't call, ourselves. Blame offers one. This story offers a different place: what happened, held without a verdict.
screen: `THE DISH ONLY HE ATE.` · `SOMEONE MIGHT BLAME THE COOK.` · `TWO OFFERINGS, EQUAL FRUIT.` · `A CAUSE IS NOT A CULPRIT.` · then, large: `NO ONE TO BLAME.`

segments.voice: Let one blame come to mind. Something small is fine: a late delivery, a coworker's slip, something you've been holding against yourself. Breathe in and name what happened, plainly, the way the sutta names the meal and then the sickness. Breathe out and set down the word fault, just for now. You aren't deciding that nobody was responsible. You're only letting the event be an event. If the blame comes back, notice it, and set it down again. The bell holds the time.
Cunda, the cook who served the Buddha's last meal and was told to carry no remorse: a cause is not a culprit. Today's word.
Your line: held without a verdict. Today, when you catch yourself asking whose fault something is, ask first what happened, and stop there for a moment. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

screen: `DAY 767 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: REBIRTH, AS THEY TEACH IT.`

768.title: Rebirth, as they teach it
768.hook: Buddhists teach rebirth shaped by karma, without a fixed soul passing on
768.howItsDone: Buddhists teach rebirth through talks, texts and funeral rites; in some Buddhist communities, families make offerings and dedicate merit to the person who has died, and the details of the teaching differ from school to school.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha sent word to Cunda the cook. Your line was held without a verdict. Did you set one blame down? Today, what Buddhists teach comes after a death. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

A king has a monk cornered, or thinks he does. In an old Buddhist dialogue called the Questions of King Milinda, the king asks the monk Nagasena: if there's no lasting self, then who, exactly, is reborn? It's a fair question. Buddhists teach rebirth: that after death, life goes on in a new existence, shaped by karma. They also teach that there's no unchanging soul underneath it all. Today: how Buddhists hold both at once, as they teach it.
screen: `A KING ASKS A MONK.` → `WHO IS REBORN?` → `NO FIXED SOUL.`

segments.voice: First, karma. In Buddhist teaching, karma is intentional action: what a person chooses, and what follows from the choice. The Dhammapada opens with it. Act with an evil thought, it says, and "pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage." Act with a pure thought, and happiness follows like a shadow. Actions ripen. Second, no fixed self. Buddhists teach anatta, not-self: body, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, all of it is changing, and nothing in the list is a permanent owner. So rebirth, as they teach it, isn't a soul moving to a new house. Third, the lamp. The king asks whether anything passes over from one life to the next. Nagasena answers with a picture: light one lamp from another. Does the flame travel across? No. Yet the second lamp is burning because of the first. And another: a pupil learns a verse from a teacher. Did the verse leave the teacher? No. Rebirth, Nagasena says, is like that: nothing passes over, and still something continues. Fourth, as they teach it. Buddhist schools describe the details differently; some teach an in-between state before the next life, and some do not. Buddhists today hold the teaching in different ways, some as a plain account of what happens, some mostly as a way of seeing how actions bear fruit. That is their conversation, carried on with care. Hearing it described is not being asked to believe it. It's being let into the room.
screen: `KARMA: ACTIONS RIPEN.` · `ANATTA: NO FIXED SELF.` · `A LAMP LIT FROM A LAMP.` · `SCHOOLS SAY IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `AS THEY TEACH IT.`

segments.voice: Bring your own family to mind. Not the whole family tree, just the people you grew up around. What did they say happens when someone dies? Maybe there was a clear answer. Maybe there was a silence, or several answers that didn't match. Let whatever you remember be there, without arguing with it. Then choose one person you could ask, someone who would know, or someone you've never asked. The bell holds the time.
Rebirth: the Buddhist teaching that life continues after death in a new existence shaped by karma, with no fixed soul passing on. Today's word.
Your line: as they teach it. Today, ask one person in your family what they believe happens after we die, and just listen. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

769.title: A last poem
769.hook: Japanese monks and poets wrote a short poem as death approached
769.howItsDone: In Japan, Zen monks and poets kept a custom of writing a short farewell poem, a jisei, as death approached; these poems are still collected, read and written today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rebirth, as Buddhists teach it: a lamp lit from a lamp. Your line was as they teach it. Did you ask anyone in your family? Today, from Japan, a few lines written at the end. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

A brush, a sheet of paper, and not much time. In Japan, Zen monks and poets kept a custom: as death came near, they would leave a short poem behind. It was called a jisei, a farewell poem. Not a will, not a speech, not a list of regrets. Sometimes just a picture: a field, a moon, a sound in the night. Today: what someone chooses to see when they know they're writing the last thing.
screen: `A BRUSH, NOT MUCH TIME.` → `NOT A WILL, A POEM.` → `WHAT DO YOU SEE LAST?`

segments.voice: First, the custom. A farewell poem was a way of meeting death with attention instead of only fear. Tradition says some Zen teachers were expected to leave a verse for their students, a last teaching in a handful of words. Poets took up the practice too. Second, a sickbed. The poet Matsuo Bashō walked the roads of Japan and wrote about them. He fell ill on a journey, and his students wrote down a poem from those days. In plain English, it says something like this: sick on a journey, my dreams go wandering over withered fields. That's it. No lesson about death. Just a traveler who, lying still, is still traveling in his dreams, across a winter landscape. Third, a story people tell. When his students asked for a death poem, the story goes, Bashō answered that every poem he had written was his death poem. Whether or not he said it, the idea has stayed: if any poem might be the last, each one is written with that care. Fourth, why it matters on a Tuesday. A last poem asks a simple question. If there were only a few words left, what would be worth seeing? The answer can be small, the way Bashō's was: a field, gone brown, and a traveler's dream crossing it. Writing one long before the end isn't gloomy. It's a way of finding out what you notice when you stop to look.
screen: `A FAREWELL POEM.` · `SICK ON A JOURNEY.` · `EVERY POEM A LAST POEM.` · `WHAT'S WORTH SEEING NOW?` · then, large: `A LAST POEM.`

segments.voice: Make a three-line poem, in your head or under your breath. No counting syllables, no rhyme. Look at one thing in front of you, or listen to one sound. Let the first line name it. Let the second line say what it's doing. Let the third line add one surprise, or simply where you are. Say it to yourself a few times and change a word if one feels wrong. If you'd like to keep it, write it down after the bell. The bell holds the time.
Jisei: a Japanese farewell poem, written by monks and poets as death drew near, sometimes about something small seen clearly. Today's word.
Your line: a traveler's dream crossing it. Today, write down the three lines you made, and put them somewhere you'll find them again. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

770.title: Worn clothes
770.hook: as a person casts off worn clothes, the self casts off worn bodies
770.howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home, in temples and in study groups, and verses from its second chapter, including this one, are sometimes recited in times of death and grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a jisei, a farewell poem. Your line was a traveler's dream crossing it. Did you write your three lines down? Today, the week's last day, and a turn from Buddhist voices to a Hindu one. Day seven hundred seventy.

A shirt with a frayed collar and thin elbows. Worn so long it's soft as paper. Sooner or later it gets folded and let go. The Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture spoken on a battlefield, reaches for exactly that picture when it talks about death. Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that the self sets aside worn-out bodies the way a person sets aside worn-out clothes. Today: the picture, and why it's said to a man standing between two armies.
screen: `A FRAYED SHIRT.` → `SPOKEN ON A BATTLEFIELD.` → `CLOTHES AND THE ONE WHO WEARS THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Arjuna looks across the field and sees teachers and relatives in the other army. He puts down his bow. He is grieving before a single arrow has flown. Krishna, his charioteer, whom many Hindus worship as God, begins to answer him. Second, the self. Krishna says the self is never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. A little later he adds that weapons do not cut it and fire does not burn it. Third, the clothes. Between those two teachings comes the picture. In Edwin Arnold's old English verse: "So putteth by the spirit / Lightly its garb of flesh." Clothes wear thin; the one who wears them goes on. It's a household image for one of the hardest questions people ask. Fourth, how it's read. Some Hindu teachers read the verse as comfort, and as a teaching about what in a person lasts. But notice who hears it first: not a mourner at a funeral, a man about to act. Krishna's point, in the poem, is that grief for bodies should not keep Arjuna from his duty. Some readers take the battlefield as a real war; others read it as a picture of the struggle inside a person. Both readings hear the same verse about clothes. And a look back: this week went from death recalled with each breath, to the charnel ground, strive on, no one to blame, rebirth, a last poem, and now worn clothes.

segments.voice: If there's an old piece of clothing nearby, a shirt, a scarf, a sock, take it in your hands. If not, rest a hand on the sleeve you're wearing. Fold it slowly, one edge to the other. Notice the worn places: a thin spot, a loose thread, a softness that only comes from use. Breathe while you fold. You don't have to think about death at all. Just handle something that has been worn, gently, and set it down. The bell holds the time.
Worn clothes: the Bhagavad Gita's picture of the self setting aside a worn body the way a person sets aside worn clothing. Today's word.
Your line: garb of flesh. Today, when you get dressed or undressed, let one garment remind you of the verse, and of the one who wears it. Day seven hundred seventy.
